overview: Identify hail and wind damage accurately, differentiate from wear, and document collateral to build strong claims.
learningObjectives: Recognize hail and wind indicators on shingles
Differentiate storm damage from normal wear

sections.title: Damage Types Overview
sections.content:
### 🌨️ Hail Damage

Example roof damage - impact patterns

Example roof damage - shingle surface

Example roof damage - close-up detail

#### What to Look For: - Circular bruising/divots on shingles - Loss of granules exposing asphalt mat - Shiny spots where granules are gone - Damage to vents, flashing, gutters (matching damage) - Dented AC units, downspouts #### How to Document: - **Test square:** Use penny for size reference - Take 5-7 photos per damaged area - Show both close-up and context shots - Photograph matching damage on ground items

sections.title: Wind Damage
sections.content:
### 💨 Wind Damage

Missing shingles blown off by wind

Lifted and creased shingles

Torn shingles at edges and ridges

#### What to Look For: - Missing shingles (blown off) - Lifted/creased shingles - Torn shingles (especially at edges) - Exposed underlayment - Damaged or missing ridge caps #### How to Document: - Wide shots showing missing sections - Close-ups of lifted tabs - Document direction (shows wind pattern) - Check all edges and corners first

sections.title: Collateral Assessment
sections.content:
### 🎯 Collateral Damage

Example collateral damage on exterior surfaces

Example impact damage on property

Example secondary storm damage

#### Why Collateral Damage Matters: Collateral damage strengthens your claim by proving storm impact across multiple surfaces. - **Metal Items:** Dented gutters, downspouts, vents, flashing, AC units - **Soft Items:** Window screens with pitting, vinyl siding damage - **Ground Items:** Damaged deck railings, mailboxes, outdoor furniture - **Key Point:** Insurance can't argue "normal wear" when brand-new items show obvious impact damage

sections.title: The Test Square Method
sections.content:
## 📐 The "Test Square" Method Insurance companies require a **test square** - a 10x10 ft area with minimum damage counts:

Example damage documentation method

Example test square area measurement

Example damage reference documentation

### Requirements: - **Hail:** Minimum 8-10 hits per 100 sq ft (varies by carrier) - **Location:** Choose south or west-facing slope (most sun exposure = most damage) - **Documentation:** Circle damage with chalk, photograph from multiple angles - **Why it matters:** This determines if they'll approve full replacement vs. repair

sections.title: Storm vs Non-Storm Damage
sections.content:
## ⚠️ Storm Damage vs. Non-Storm Damage It's vital to differentiate between actual storm damage and other roof issues.

✅ Storm Damage (Qualifying)

Example storm damage - qualifying impacts

Wind: Lifted/creased shingles

  • Hail Damage: Circular "bruises" or divots where granules are knocked off, often with a soft or spongy feel
  • Wind Damage: Lifted, creased, or missing shingles from strong winds
  • Why Qualifying: These are direct results of weather events covered by insurance

❌ Non-Storm Damage (Non-Qualifying)

Example non-qualifying damage reference

Example wear pattern reference

Example deterioration reference

  • Blistering: Looks like bubbles on shingle surface - a manufacturing defect, not storm damage
  • Cracking: Age-related deterioration appearing as splintering or straight lines
  • Granule Loss: General, even loss of granules due to age, not concentrated spots like hail hits
  • Why Non-Qualifying: These are wear-and-tear issues, not covered by storm damage insurance

sections.title: Documentation Strategy
sections.content:
## Documentation Strategy Sequence

Follow this exact order for professional, adjuster-ready documentation:

1. **Property ID:** House number, full front view
2. **Overview Shots:** All four elevations of the home
3. **Elevation Collateral:** Gutters, siding, windows from each side
4. **Roof Overview:** Wide shots of each slope
5. **Damage Markup:** Circle hail hits with chalk, slash wind damage
6. **Close-ups:** Individual damage photos with size reference (penny/quarter)
7. **Granule Loss:** Gutters and downspouts filled with granules
